opening.headline: Learn why everything from researching data to writing a report ends up being sloppy in the middle when you do it all at once, and learn how to divide complex tasks into steps.
body: If you ask, “Research the market data for a new product, summarize it, and write a report all at once,” you are likely to get a result with a plausible introduction and conclusion, but a thin middle part of the basis. What's even more frustrating is that I can't tell where the mistake came from, so I have to start over from the beginning.

In this class, we will look at how to divide a large task into small steps and give separate instructions for each step, and how to follow through with a person checking the results of each step. Next, we will check the tips for dividing instructions, context, and input into separators and tags, and the standards for distinguishing between tasks that can be ordered at once and tasks that must be divided.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the effects of dividing work into steps
Can distinguish between tasks to be done at once and tasks to be divided into tasks.

screens.title: I ordered it at once and the middle part was poor.
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the context description below to see a short description. Check them out one by one.

visual.alt: Below the long request speech bubble, there is a report outline with a thick introduction and conclusion and a thin middle.
labels: Research and summarize new product market data and write a report at once
I don't know where it went wrong

data.text: The request was "Investigate market data on a new product, summarize it, and prepare a report using at once." The returned report was Introduction and conclusion and seemed plausible, but the underlying data source middle survey part was insufficient. We cannot determine where the error occurred—whether due to inadequate research, omission during summarization, or oversight during writing—so ultimately, from scratch again must be assigned. In this course, we learn how to assign tasks involving at once and how to divide tasks appropriately to avoid such issues.

terms.tip: This method involves researching, summarizing, and writing all in one request. It seems simple, but there is no way to check the intermediate process.
This is the back and forth of the report. The model is easy to use as a general framework, so it seems plausible even if there is insufficient evidence.
This is the part where evidence to support the conclusion is included. If you have too many things to do at once, you may not have enough attention to devote to this area.
This is an expensive method to choose when you do not know where the error originated. By breaking it down into steps, you can only fix the step where the problem occurred.

screens.outro: First, let me recall an experience where I had to divide a large task into pieces.

screens.title: Think about an experience where you were entrusted with splitting a large task into pieces.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. There are no fields to enter or submit, so think about it first and then click it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced something that worked better when you divided up a large task?
items.answer: The same goes for people. If you entrust a large task all at once, you won't know the progress until you receive the results. If you entrust it in chunks, you can check it at each step and change direction. The same method works for models.

items.prompt: When you split it, were you able to check and fix it?
items.answer: This is the biggest advantage of dividing the steps. Check the result of step 1, and if it is wrong, correct step 1 and proceed again. If you go to the next step with an error, the error will spread backwards.

items.prompt: Where does a problem arise when you leave it all at once?
items.answer: It usually occurs at an intermediate stage. The beginning and end are noticeable, but the middle is difficult to see, so any inaccuracies are discovered late. By then, it has already become difficult to find the cause.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by looking at how to divide the work.

screens.title: Work breakdown and step-by-step instructions
screens.lead: Select and expand each item to see how complex tasks are broken down. Open them all and compare.

visual.alt: A diagram in which one large prompt is divided into numbered smaller prompts, forming a chain.
labels: The previous output is the next input

items.title: Break down instructions one by one
items.body: The Gemini guide explains that when dealing with complex prompts, if a prompt contains multiple instructions, you can create one prompt for each instruction. And you can choose which prompt to process based on the user's input. It is easier for the model to focus on each instruction rather than asking it to do several things at once.

items.title: Chain prompts
items.body: For tasks that require multiple steps in sequence, create a prompt for each step and follow them in order. The Gemini guide explains that the output of the previous prompt in the chain becomes the input to the next prompt, and the output of the last prompt becomes the final result. The research results are used as material for the summary, and the summary is used as material for the draft.

items.title: Divide and merge in parallel
items.body: Independent parts can be processed separately and then the results can be collected. The Gemini guide introduces you to performing different operations on different parts of your data in parallel and combining the results. For example, long material is divided into chapters, each summarized, and then combined.

items.title: Write steps as a numbered list
items.body: You can write steps even within a single request. When order or completeness is important, Claude Guide recommends writing down instructions as sequential steps, either as a numbered list or as bullet points. If the steps are few and independent of each other, this method is sufficient.

items.title: Focus on subtasks
items.body: Claude's consistency guide explains that breaking complex tasks into smaller, consistent subtasks ensures that each subtask receives the model's full attention, reducing errors. The reason for dividing the work is for quality, not convenience.

screens.outro: Let's look at the actual conversation flow divided into four stages, from investigation to review.

screens.title: Four-step conversation flow from investigation to review
screens.lead: Select each tab to view the step-by-step request, expected output, and what the human will check.

visual.alt: A flow of four conversation cards connected by arrows: Research, Summary, Draft, and Review.
labels: Modify the draft if it is out of sync

tabs.label: Step 1 Investigation
tabs.body:
Request: “Please tabulate the names, prices, and key features of three competing products from the data below. Leave blank for information not included.”

Expected output: A list of data and a table containing only the key facts.
What people should check: Do the prices and features in the table match the data? The facts at this stage are checked most thoroughly as they are the basis for all subsequent stages.

tabs.label: Step 2 Summary
tabs.body:
Request: “Using only the facts identified in the table above, please summarize three points of differentiation that give our product an edge.”

Expected Output: Three differentiators based on the facts in the table.
What people should check: Is the summary mixed with information that is not in the table? Let's see if the restriction of writing only confirmed facts was followed.

tabs.label: Stage 3 Draft
tabs.body:
Request: “Based on the summary, please write a draft of the new product plan in the order of the table of contents. Please do not include any figures that are not in the summary.”

Expected output: A draft plan aligned with the table of contents.
What people should check: Are the structure and tone of the draft fit for purpose? Since the underlying facts have already been identified in the previous step, you can focus on the flow of the text at this stage.

tabs.label: Step 4 Review
tabs.body:
Request: “Please point out any areas in the draft that are inconsistent with the Stage 1 table or Stage 2 summary.”

Expected output: A list of mismatched sentences and their reasons.
What people should check: Is the point pointed out actually a problem? Between each step, a person checks the results, and if there are any problems, only that step is corrected and re-run.

screens.outro: Let's look at tips for distinguishing instructions and materials when dividing steps, and criteria for deciding whether or not to divide them.

screens.title: Separators and tags to select tasks to entrust at once
screens.lead: Press the switch to compare the flow and extent of error spread when doing the same task at once and when doing it separately.

states.label: Do it all at once
states.body:
Research, summary, draft, and review in one request. This method is most efficient for simple, one-time calls, few steps, and low error costs. For example, trimming short sentences or summarizing a paragraph.

However, in tasks where subsequent tasks depend on previous results, mistakes in the middle spread backwards. Since you can't tell where something went wrong, you have to start over again, and the cost of doing it again is high.

states.label: Divide the order
states.body:
Send a separate request for each step and check the results. The number of calls increases, but errors can be caught in the middle, and only the step where the problem occurred can be corrected and rerun. It is suitable for tasks in which subsequent tasks depend on previous results, and tasks in which error costs are high.

As you break down the steps, it becomes important to distinguish between instructions and materials. Claude's guide explains that wrapping instructions, context, and input in tags such as <instructions>, <context>, and <input> respectively reduces misunderstandings. The OpenAI guide tells you that you can delimit the prompt with Markdown titles, lists, and XML tags, and that you use tags to indicate where the reference material begins and ends. This is especially useful when putting the output of a previous step into the next request.

screens.outro: Now let’s apply it to the case of dividing a new product plan into four stages.

screens.title: Explanation: Dividing a new product plan into 4 steps, steps 1 and 2
screens.lead: The instructor shows step by step the process of dividing the work of a new product plan. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Criteria for confirming and dividing tasks
steps.body: The task is a new product plan. It is a structure in which the market research results become the basis for the summary, and the summary becomes the basis for the draft, and the subsequent work depends on the previous results. Since it is easy for mistakes to spread later, I think it would be appropriate to distribute them.

steps.title: Step 1: Market Research
steps.body: The first request is, “Please tabulate the prices and features of three competing products.” Narrow the scope so this step focuses solely on gathering facts. Information that cannot be incorrect, such as price and features, begins in this table, so people check it against the data.

steps.title: Proceed only after confirmation
steps.body: Only after a person confirms the results of step 1 does it proceed to step 2. If you skip this check, the steps lose their meaning. If an error is found, only step 1 is corrected and received again.

steps.title: Step 2: Summary
steps.body: The second request is, “From the table above, please select three points that differentiate our product from the table above.” At this time, separate the table from step 1 from the instructions by placing it in the <context> tag. It prevents the model from making things up by restricting the use of information that is not in the table.

steps.title: Instructor's explanation
steps.body: Each step produces one output, and the output becomes the input for the next step. If I had ordered it all at once, I wouldn't have been able to see the differences from this table. Next we will cover Stage 3 Drafting and Stage 4 Review.

screens.outro: Next, we'll look at the drafting and review stages, and how to catch errors along the way.

screens.title: Commentary: Drafting and reviewing, catching errors along the way.
screens.lead: The table below outlines the four steps with confirmation points. Read along the lines to see what they check at each step and how they respond when problems arise.

data.notes: For example, if a pricing error for a competitive product is identified in step 1, only that step is corrected and the next steps are rerun. If it had been done all at once, it would have been difficult to find where the error originated. The instructor's evaluation criterion is whether there are deliverables to check at each step.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the contents of this class.

screens.title: Standard for sharing
screens.lead: I will organize the contents so far as a basis for deciding whether to share or not.

paragraphs: Divide big tasks into steps and give separate instructions for each step. Then, you will have output to check for each step, and even if an error occurs, only that step can be corrected. The “poor mid-level report” I saw at first was a problem that occurred because the intermediate steps were not separately confirmed.

But you don't have to share everything. Tasks with few steps and low error costs can be done in one go. There are two questions that determine whether to share. Does the subsequent task depend on the previous result? Is the cost of doing it again high when an intermediate mistake spreads backwards?

When dividing, separate instructions, context, and input with tags or titles. When putting the results of the previous step into the next request, the boundaries must be clear so the model does not misunderstand the material as instructions. When I look for points in my work where the results depend on previous steps, I see where to divide.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: By breaking it down into steps, you can catch errors in the middle. However, it is meaningful only if a person checks between steps.

glossary.def: Breaking down large tasks into small, ordered steps.
This method connects the output of the previous stage to the input of the next stage.
A person checks the output of each step and, if necessary, corrects only that step.
An XML tag or Markdown title that delineates instructions, context, and boundaries of input.

misconceptions.myth: It is more efficient if you do it all at once.
misconceptions.fact: Although calls are reduced, if an intermediate error spreads, the cost can be high as it has to be started again from the beginning. It is safer to split tasks that depend on the results of the previous task.

misconceptions.myth: The more you share, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Tasks with few steps and low error costs can be done in one go. Splitting increases calls, so split only where necessary.

misconceptions.myth: Tags and separators are just decoration.
misconceptions.fact: Reduce model misunderstanding by distinguishing between instructions, data, and input. This is especially effective when passing over the output of the previous step.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Divide big tasks into steps and give separate instructions for each step.
By dividing it into steps, you can catch errors in the middle and fix only those steps.
If the subsequent task depends on the previous result and the error cost is high, split it up, and do simple tasks at once.
Instructions, context, and input are separated by tags or titles.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: At what point in my work should I divide tasks?

checks.q: What is the correct order to divide a complex report task into steps?
items: Research: List data and select only key facts
Draft: Write a draft report based on the summary.
Review: Point out where the draft diverges from the summary.
checks.explain: Since the results of the previous stage become the input for the next stage, it proceeds in the order of research, summary, draft, and review, with people checking between stages.
checks.intro: Try putting them in order, remembering the order of division into steps. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: What is the biggest advantage of handing out new product plans rather than all at once?
options: The time is always shortened by reducing the number of calls.
You can find errors at intermediate stages and correct only those stages.
No need for people to check each step
There is no need to distinguish between instructions and context.
checks.explain: When a later task depends on the previous result, you can find out where the error started by dividing it, and problems such as a pricing error can be rerun by correcting only that step.

wrong.0: If you divide it, the number of calls actually increases.
wrong.2: A person checks the results of each step before moving on.
wrong.3: Instructions, context, and input are separated by tags.

checks.intro: Remember the reason for sharing and choose the appropriate option. Results are not recorded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's unfortunate, but other options are better.
